title: Boredom
hookLine: boredom as something to look at
tomorrow: how does a practice survive a brand-new schedule?

lines: ESCAPE IT, OR LOOK AT IT?
cards: Boredom used to mean waiting for a bus. Now it barely lasts before a thumb finds a screen. Mai's sits have gone gray: no struggle, no peace, just a long flat middle.
Then Ava mentions that her church youth group heard about monks in the early Christian desert who had a name for this exact feeling, the restless, nothing-is-happening heaviness of midday.
So, the old question, asked in two traditions at once: is boredom something to escape, or something to look at?

teach.b: The Buddhist answer comes from a nun named Dhammadinna. A lay follower, Visakha, who tradition says had once been her husband, brings her a list of questions, and the Majjhima Nikaya keeps her answers.
One is about the feeling that's neither pleasant nor painful, the flat middle.
She says it's pleasant when it's known, and painful when it isn't. Later Visakha tells the Buddha everything she said, and the Buddha says he'd have answered the same way.
One way Buddhist teachers read boredom: a neutral feeling nobody is looking at, so all we want is out. The practice turns toward it instead. Where does it sit in the body?
Does it shift? It arises, and it passes, like everything else. Known, the gray can turn quiet, even restful.
Ava's tradition has its own version.

teach.h: ABBA MOSES: SIT IN YOUR CELL.
teach.b: The desert monks called that restless midday heaviness acedia, and one of them, Abba Moses, told a struggling brother, in effect: go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything.

teach.h: BOTH SAY STAY. THEY STAY DIFFERENTLY.
teach.b: Both say stay; don't run. The honest difference: for the desert monks, the cell is where you wait before God, and the restlessness is a temptation to stand against.
For Dhammadinna, the feeling itself is what you look at, until it's known.

how: In Buddhist meditation, boredom is often treated as something to observe: practitioners notice the flat, neutral feeling, where it shows up in the body and how it changes, rather than escaping it.

o: a flat, restless feeling worth looking at closely
a sign you've picked the wrong meditation
a punishment for being lazy in your practice

games.q: the gray middle — tap the pairs.
p: pleasant when known, painful when not
sit in your cell; it will teach you
the desert monks' word for that heaviness

s: Buddhist practice is meant to make boredom go away
the move is to look at it: a neutral feeling, once known, can turn pleasant.
the Buddha said he'd have answered Visakha just as Dhammadinna did
her answers stand as teaching in the Majjhima Nikaya.
the desert monks and Dhammadinna teach the same thing in the same way
both say stay. the monks stay before God and resist a temptation; Dhammadinna looks at the feeling itself.

games.q: a long car ride, your phone is dead, and there's nothing but the window. what would Dhammadinna's answer have you try?
o: sleep through it so the time goes faster.
look closely at the flat feeling itself until it's known.
plan out your whole week to fill the empty time.
games.why: a neutral feeling is pleasant when it's known and painful when it isn't. look, and the gray can turn quiet.

practice: Close your eyes, and don't fix anything. When the flat feeling comes, look straight at it: is it in the jaw, the chest, behind the eyes? Heavy or light, still or itchy?
Watch it the way you'd watch a cloud, until it changes.

wordCard.voice: Boredom: often a neutral feeling no one is looking at. Dhammadinna said a feeling like that is pleasant once it's known.

orig.note: Pali: feeling, the felt tone of an experience: pleasant, painful, or neither. Boredom often lives in the third.

carryVoice: Look at it: the flat gray middle, once it's known, can turn quiet. Catch you tomorrow.
